content: Epithelial ovarian cancer is diagnosed in over 200,000 women globally each year. Among these, 10% to 20% of cases are detected at an early stage, when the likelihood of achieving a cure is relatively high. For early-stage disease, specifically FIGO stage I and IIa, the standard treatment involves surgical removal of the tumor. This is often followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, which is chemotherapy administered after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence. Clinical trials have demonstrated that platinum-based chemotherapy provides an overall survival benefit in this context. However, the precise role of adjuvant chemotherapy, as well as its effectiveness in specific subgroups of patients with varying prognoses, remains to be fully clarified. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate whether adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery improves survival outcomes compared to observation alone, where chemotherapy is reserved for cases of disease recurrence. Additionally, the review aimed to determine whether certain clinical subgroups, defined by factors such as histological subtype or the completeness of surgical staging, derive greater or lesser benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy. To gather evidence, an extensive electronic search was conducted using databases such as the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to March 2015. The search strategy incorporated both free-text terms and medical subject headings (MeSH). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer, staged via laparotomy, were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the included studies. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models, including subgroup analyses. The original Cochrane review, published in 2009, included five RCTs with a total of 1,277 participants. In this 2015 update, no new studies met the inclusion criteria, but additional long-term data (10-year follow-up) from a previously included study (ICON1) were incorporated. Four studies were included in the meta-analyses, and these were deemed to have a low risk of bias. The majority of participants (>95%) had stage I ovarian cancer. Meta-analysis of five-year data from three studies demonstrated that women who received adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy had significantly better overall survival (OS) compared to those who did not receive chemotherapy. The hazard ratio (HR) for OS was 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 0.93), based on data from 1,008 women across three studies, with no evidence of statistical heterogeneity (I² = 0%). Similarly, meta-analysis of five-year data from four studies showed improved progression-free survival (PFS) in the chemotherapy group, with an HR of 0.67 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.84), based on data from 1,170 women, again with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). These survival benefits persisted over time. At 10 years, the HR for OS was 0.72 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.92) and for PFS was 0.67 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.83), based on data from 925 women in two studies. The risk of death at 10 years was lower in the adjuvant chemotherapy group, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.76 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.94), as was the risk of disease progression (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.87). Both findings were supported by high-quality evidence. Subgroup analyses suggested that women with high-risk disease might derive the greatest benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy. However, the data were insufficient to confirm or exclude survival benefits in women with lower-risk disease or those who underwent optimal surgical staging. Additionally, there was a lack of data to compare adverse events and long-term risks between the chemotherapy and observation groups. In conclusion, high-quality evidence supports the use of adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy to improve survival outcomes in women with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer (FIGO stage I/IIa). However, the magnitude of benefit for women with lowand intermediate-risk disease remains uncertain. Decisions regarding the use of adjuvant chemotherapy in these patients should consider this uncertainty, as well as the potential for adverse effects. For women with lower-risk disease, treatment decisions should be individualized, taking into account specific patient factors.
